newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen mission seeks release of Russian soldiers.
newsitem.headline: Chechen mission seeks release of Russian soldiers.

text.p: Chechnya's separatist leaders, anxious to keep the region's delicate peace process on track, dispatched a mission on Monday to negotiate the release of 21 Russian soldiers held captive by a radical rebel commander.
Moscow has warned that the incident could halt its withdrawal of troops from the breakaway region as agreed in a peace deal it made with the Chechen separatists.
However Salman Raduyev, whose men seized the troops on Saturday, laid out conditions for their release and indicated they would probably not be freed before Tuesday at the earliest.

Raduyev told Reuters he was ready to free 10 of his captives provided that a Russian commander in the region publicly apologised for preventing his men entering the neighbouring region of Dagestan last Saturday.
He said he hoped to exchange the remaining 11 captives for Chechen prisoners of war still held by the Russians.

Major-General Vladimir Dmitrin, commander of the Interior Ministry troops in Chechnya, told Interfax news agency Monday's mission, comprising senior Russian and Chechen officials, was heading for the village of Novy Gerzel to meet Raduyev.

The village is on the border with Dagestan where the Russian troops were seized on Saturday by up to 60 armed Chechen fighters after they refused them permission to cross the border to attend a conference.
Dmitrin was optimistic that the mission would secure the release of his men and their weapons, Interfax said.
Interfax quoted another Russian commander, Vladimir Sukhoruchenko, as saying the incident should not be blown out of proportion.
He noted that Raduyev, a radical who led a hostage-taking raid into Dagestan last January, had no link with the Chechen separatists' political and military leadership.
"I hope that we all have enough sober sense not to let this incident harm the peace process," Interfax quoted Sukhoruchenko as saying.

Nevertheless the seizure of the Russian soldiers has highlighted continuing tensions in Chechnya, still devastated by 21 months of fierce fighting between Russian troops and Islamic separatists that came to a halt with the August 31 peace deal.

The accord defers for five years a final decision on Chechnya's political status. The rebels still insist on full independence but Moscow hopes to persuade them with economic inducements to stay within the Russian Federation.
Raduyev told Russian television on Monday that he would not participate in the peace process while Russia refused to recognise his oil-rich region's independence.
"I shall struggle with Russia for full independence, however long it takes. My army and I will only make peace when the independence of our state is officially recognised," he said.
Last month President Boris Yeltsin agreed to pull out Russia's last troops from Chechnya, two years after he ordered a full-scale military assualt to crush its independence bid.

On Monday Interfax said around 1,000 troops had left Chechnya since Yeltsin's decree on November 29. Tass quoted Ministry of Defence officials as saying it would take more than a month to withdraw all its troops.
Chechnya's rebel leaders are anxious to ensure that the troops leave their region before presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled for January 27.
They have denounced hostage-taking incidents like Raduyev's in the past and have moved to resolve them quickly.
